content.text: How to check it worked

items: The report shows Bills 2799.00, Food 2350.50, Travel 760.75, Fun 450.00 and All 6360.25.
The biggest expense is `Electricity 1800.0`.
The program still works after you add rows with a new category.

steps.say: The data starts in a CSV file with one expense on each row.
csv.DictReader reads each row as a dictionary, with the column names as keys.
The loop converts amounts to numbers and adds them to the total of each category.
The totals are sorted from biggest to smallest and printed with each category share.

faqs.q: Why not just use a spreadsheet?
faqs.a: A spreadsheet is fine for one-off work. A Python script is better when you repeat the same job every week, when the file is very large, or when you want the steps written down and checked.

faqs.q: When should I use pandas?
faqs.a: When you work with large tables, many columns or need joins and charts. It saves code, but learn plain Python first so you understand what it does.

lessons.title: Automate Boring Tasks: Organise Files and Folders with Python
lessons.metaTitle: Python Automation: Tidy Files and Folders
lessons.description: Use pathlib and shutil to sort a messy folder by file type, rename and move files safely, test on practice data first and avoid deleting anything by mistake.

content.text: Many people first feel the power of programming when Python does a dull job for them: sorting a downloads folder, renaming hundreds of photos, collecting files from many folders into one place. The tools are `pathlib` for paths and `shutil` for moving and copying. Because these programs change things on your computer, we will go carefully, test on practice files first and build in safety checks.
Safety first

items: **Practise on a copy or on practice files,** never on your only copy of something important.
**Print what you would do before you do it.** A *dry run* shows the plan and changes nothing. When it looks right, switch to the real run.
**Never overwrite silently.** Check whether the destination exists, and skip or rename.
**Avoid deleting.** Moving files into a folder is safer than removing them. If you do use `rmtree` or `unlink`, be very sure of the path.
**Keep a record** of what you changed, even a simple printed list.

content.text: The program

The program below creates its own practice folder with seven small files, sorts them by type into sub-folders, shows the final layout and removes the practice folder at the end. Read it before you run it.

import shutil
from pathlib import Path

# Make a practice folder with some untidy files
folder = Path("downloads_demo")
folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
for name in ["cv.pdf", "photo1.jpg", "photo2.JPG", "notes.txt", "budget.xlsx", "report.pdf", "README"]:
    (folder / name).write_text("demo", encoding="utf-8")

groups = {
    ".pdf": "documents", ".txt": "documents",
    ".jpg": "images", ".png": "images",
    ".xlsx": "spreadsheets",
}

for item in sorted(folder.iterdir()):
    if not item.is_file():
        continue
    target_name = groups.get(item.suffix.lower())
    if target_name is None:
        print("Left alone:", item.name)
        continue
    target = folder / target_name
    target.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    destination = target / item.name.lower()
    if destination.exists():
        print("Skipped (exists):", item.name)
        continue
    shutil.move(str(item), destination)
    print(f"Moved {item.name} -> {target_name}/")

for path in sorted(folder.rglob("*")):
    print(path.relative_to(folder))

shutil.rmtree(folder)

Left alone: README
Moved budget.xlsx -> spreadsheets/
Moved cv.pdf -> documents/
Moved notes.txt -> documents/
Moved photo1.jpg -> images/
Moved photo2.JPG -> images/
Moved report.pdf -> documents/
README
documents
documents/cv.pdf
documents/notes.txt
documents/report.pdf
images
images/photo1.jpg
images/photo2.jpg
spreadsheets
spreadsheets/budget.xlsx
What happens

items: `folder.iterdir()` lists everything in the folder. We loop over `sorted(...)` so the order is the same on every computer. `item.is_file()` skips folders.

`item.suffix` is the file ending, such as `.pdf`. `.lower()` makes `.JPG` and `.jpg` the same. A dictionary maps each ending to a group name. `groups.get(...)` returns `None` for unknown endings, like the file `README`, which is left alone.
`target.mkdir(exist_ok=True)` creates the group folder if it does not exist, and does nothing if it does.
Before moving, we check `destination.exists()`. If a file with that name is already there, the program skips it and says so, so nothing is overwritten.
`shutil.move` moves the file. The name is made lower case in the new place, which is why `photo2.JPG` became `photo2.jpg`.
`folder.rglob("*")` walks through all files and folders below, and `relative_to` shortens the printed paths.

content.text: Turning it into a real tool

To use the idea on a real folder, change the `folder` line to the path you want, for example `Path.home() / "Downloads"`, remove the lines that create the practice files and the final `rmtree`, and add the dry-run switch below. Run it in dry-run mode first and read the plan.

DRY_RUN = True   # change to False only after you have read the plan

if DRY_RUN:
    print(f"Would move {item.name} -> {target_name}/")
else:
    target.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    shutil.move(str(item), destination)
    print(f"Moved {item.name} -> {target_name}/")
More ideas for automation

items: **Rename in bulk:** add a date to file names, replace spaces with underscores, or number photos in order. Use `item.rename(new_path)` or `item.with_name(new_name)`.
**Find files:** `folder.rglob("*.pdf")` finds every PDF in all sub-folders.
**Merge CSV files:** loop over files with `rglob`, read each with `csv`, and write one combined file.
**Clean old files:** list files older than 90 days using `item.stat().st_mtime`. Print them first, and move them to an archive folder before deciding to delete.
**Make backups:** `shutil.copytree` copies a whole folder, and `shutil.make_archive` makes a zip.

content.text: Running a script on a schedule

Once a script works, you can have the computer run it automatically. On Windows, Task Scheduler does this. On macOS and Linux, `cron` does it. First make sure that the script works when it is started from any folder, which means using full paths, and that it writes a log file, so you can see what happened while you were away.
Working with spreadsheets and documents

Python can also read and write Excel files with the `openpyxl` package, and Word files with `python-docx`. They need installing with pip inside a virtual environment, as shown in lesson 10. The idea is the same as with CSV: read the data, process it with loops and dictionaries, and write a result. Check each package's own documentation, because details change between versions.

Even a small mistake in a file script can move many files to the wrong place. That is the reason for dry runs and for practising on copies. If you ever move files by mistake, do not run the script again. Stop and look at what changed first.

faqs.q: Is it safe to let Python move and delete files?
faqs.a: It is safe if you test on copies, run a dry run first, avoid overwriting, and move files to an archive instead of deleting them. A mistake in a script can change many files at once.

faqs.q: What is the difference between pathlib and os.path?
faqs.a: pathlib is the newer, object-based way to work with paths, and it is easier to read. os.path is the older function-based way. Both work, and new code usually prefers pathlib.

lessons.title: Final Project: A Command Line Expense Tracker, Tests and Next Steps
lessons.description: Build a complete command line expense tracker with argparse, JSON storage, error handling and unit tests, then plan your next steps in Python.

content.text: In this last lesson, you join everything into one useful program: an expense tracker that you run from the terminal. It adds expenses, lists them and shows totals by category. It saves data in a JSON file, checks the input, reports errors in a friendly way and has unit tests. The program uses functions, dictionaries, files, exceptions and the standard library, which are the skills you practised in the earlier lessons.
Plan before you code

items: **Data:** a list of expenses, each a dictionary with an id, an amount, a category and a note. Stored in a JSON file.
**Commands:** `add`, `list`, `total`.
**Functions:** `load` and `save` for the file, `add_expense` to check and add, `totals_by_category` to calculate, and `main` to connect the command line to these.
**Rules:** an amount must be above zero. Category names are stored in title case, so `food` and `Food` are the same.
**Safety:** a missing file means an empty list, and bad input gives a clear message, not a traceback.

content.text: The program
Notice that most of the logic is in small functions that do not print anything. That makes them easy to test. The `main` function is the only one that talks to the user.
Understanding argparse

items: `argparse` reads the command line and builds the help text for you. Run `python l15_tracker.py --help` to see it.
`add_subparsers` creates commands. Each command, `add`, `list` and `total`, has its own arguments.
`type=float` makes argparse convert the amount and show an error if it is not a number. That is input validation that you did not have to write.
`nargs="?"` makes the note optional, with an empty text as the default.
`--file` lets you choose where the data is kept. We use it in the test run below, so it does not touch your real data.

content.text: Run it

$ python l15_tracker.py --file demo.json list
No expenses yet
$ python l15_tracker.py --file demo.json add 250 food "Lunch"
Saved #1: 250.00 on Food
$ python l15_tracker.py --file demo.json add 120.5 travel Metro
Saved #2: 120.50 on Travel
$ python l15_tracker.py --file demo.json add 99 food "Snacks"
Saved #3: 99.00 on Food
$ python l15_tracker.py --file demo.json list
  1  Food       250.00  Lunch
  2  Travel     120.50  Metro
  3  Food        99.00  Snacks
$ python l15_tracker.py --file demo.json total
Food       349.00
Travel     120.50
All        469.50
$ python l15_tracker.py --file demo.json add -5 food
Error: Amount must be more than zero
(exit code 1)
$ python l15_tracker.py --file demo.json add abc food
usage: l15_tracker.py add [-h] amount category [note]
l15_tracker.py add: error: argument amount: invalid float value: 'abc'
(exit code 2)

items: The first call shows `No expenses yet`, because the file does not exist yet, and `load` returned an empty list.
Each `add` prints the id and the saved values. The category `food` was saved as `Food`.
The `list` output is aligned with f-string formatting. The `total` output is sorted from the biggest to the smallest, with an `All` line that you can check by hand: 349.00 plus 120.50 is 469.50.
A negative amount is rejected by our own check, and the exit code is 1. A non-number is rejected by `argparse` with exit code 2. Exit codes let other programs tell whether yours worked.

content.text: Test it with unittest

Tests are small programs that check your code. When you change the code later, you run the tests, and they tell you quickly if you broke something. `unittest` is part of the standard library. Each method that starts with `test` is one check. `assertEqual` compares an actual value with the one you expect. `assertRaises` checks that an error happens when it should.

import unittest
from l15_tracker import add_expense, totals_by_category


class TrackerTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_add_expense_sets_id_and_title_case(self):
        items = []
        item = add_expense(items, 250, "food", "Lunch")
        self.assertEqual(item["id"], 1)
        self.assertEqual(item["category"], "Food")

    def test_zero_amount_is_rejected(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            add_expense([], 0, "Food")

    def test_totals_are_grouped_and_sorted(self):
        items = []
        add_expense(items, 100, "Travel")
        add_expense(items, 300, "Food")
        add_expense(items, 50, "Travel")
        self.assertEqual(totals_by_category(items), {"Food": 300, "Travel": 150})


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()
python -m unittest -v test_l15_tracker

test_add_expense_sets_id_and_title_case ... ok
test_totals_are_grouped_and_sorted ... ok
test_zero_amount_is_rejected ... ok

Ran 3 tests

OK

The real output also shows the timing and slightly longer test names, and the order is alphabetical. The tests work because the logic is in functions that do not print. This is the main lesson of the project: separate the thinking from the talking.
Ideas to extend the project

items: Add a `delete` command, and a `--month` option for `list`.
Add the date to each expense with `datetime.date.today().isoformat()`.
Export a CSV report with the `csv` module.
Store the data in SQLite with the `sqlite3` module instead of a JSON file.
Make a small web version with Flask or FastAPI. Both are installed with pip.

content.text: Where to go next

Choose a direction and build one real project in it. For **data and analysis**, learn `pandas`, `matplotlib` and basic statistics, and our [SQL course](/learn/sql-for-beginners) is a good companion because most data is in databases. For **web back ends**, learn Flask or FastAPI, and our [Node.js and Express course](/learn/nodejs-express-course) shows the same ideas in another language. For **automation and testing**, learn more about files, scheduling, and a test tool such as `pytest`. Our [career roadmaps](/roadmaps) show how these skills fit into jobs. Whatever you choose, build small projects regularly, read other people's code, and read the official Python documentation, which is clear and free.

Learning a language takes time, and the pace differs for everyone. Regular practice for a short time every day beats a long session once a week. No course, including this one, can promise a job. What it can do is give you real skills and projects that you can show.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The commands produce the same output as shown, apart from your own data.
All your unit tests pass, including the new ones.
A wrong command, such as a negative amount, gives a clear message and no traceback.

steps.say: You type a command, such as add 250 food, in the terminal.
argparse reads it, converts the amount to a number and shows help or an error for wrong input.
Small functions check the rules, add the expense or work out the totals. They are easy to test.
The data is saved to a JSON file, so it is still there the next time you run the program.

faqs.q: Why keep the logic in functions that do not print?
faqs.a: Functions that only take values and return results are easy to test and reuse. Put printing and user interaction in a thin outer layer such as main.

faqs.q: What should I learn after these basics?
faqs.a: Pick a direction: data (pandas), web (Flask or FastAPI), or automation and testing (pytest). Build one real project in it and read the official documentation.
